analyses.title: TaPas: Weakly Supervised Table Parsing via Pre-training
analyses.research_question: Can a pretrained transformer answer questions over tables from weak denotation supervision by directly selecting supporting cells and aggregation operations instead of generating explicit logical forms?
analyses.methodology: TAPAS extends BERT-style encoding with table-aware row, column, and numeric information so that flattened cells retain structural relationships. It is pretrained with masked-language modeling on millions of Wikipedia tables and associated text. During downstream training, the model predicts a subset of table cells and, when necessary, an aggregation operator such as SUM, COUNT, or AVERAGE using only answer denotations rather than gold logical forms. Numeric aggregation is incorporated through a differentiable objective that permits learning aggregation decisions from weak supervision.

key_findings.finding: On weakly supervised WikiSQL, TAPAS reached 83.6 test accuracy, close to the 83.9 result of the then state-of-the-art system despite not requiring logical-form supervision.
On SQA, TAPAS reached 67.2 overall accuracy and 40.4 sequence accuracy, compared with 55.1 and 28.1 respectively for the prior comparison system reported by the paper.
Transferring a TAPAS model pretrained on related table-QA data substantially improved WikiTableQuestions results, reaching 48.7 after WikiSQL transfer and 48.8 after SQA transfer.

Table-specific pretraining was important: removing it reduced development performance from 39.0 to 26.5 SQA sequence accuracy, from 84.7 to 80.8 on WikiSQL, and from 29.0 to 17.9 on WikiTableQuestions in the reported ablation.
The predicted answer is explicitly tied to selected table cells, providing cell-level evidence localization before any optional aggregation is applied.
The model's reasoning language is intentionally restricted: it selects cells and performs at most one supported aggregation rather than representing arbitrary compositional programs.

limitations: The model handles a single table at a time and requires the relevant table content to fit its input constraints, so very large tables and multi-table databases are outside its design.
Its arithmetic expressivity is limited to selecting cells followed by one simple aggregation, and it cannot directly represent nested or multi-step aggregations.
The reported WikiTableQuestions error analysis includes failures on temporal comparisons, string operations, and tables that exceed the 512-token input limit.
Cell selection supplies useful within-table provenance, but the model does not represent document pages, attachments, attachment identities, or attachment-version lineage.
raw_claims: TAPAS answers table questions without requiring annotated logical forms.
The model jointly predicts answer cells and an optional aggregation operator.
Table-aware embeddings preserve row and column structure after the table is serialized for transformer processing.
Pretraining uses Wikipedia tables together with related natural-language text.
Weak supervision is provided by final answer denotations.
Differentiable aggregation allows numeric operators to be learned without explicit operator labels.
Table-specific pretraining materially improves performance on all three evaluated downstream datasets.
Transfer from WikiSQL or SQA substantially improves performance on WikiTableQuestions.
Selected cells constitute an explicit intermediate localization of the evidence used for the answer.
The model cannot directly express arbitrary nested or compositional table operations.

analyses.title: M3Grounder: Mask-Based Multi-Span and Multi-Granular Grounding for Document QA
analyses.research_question: Can document question answering jointly generate accurate answers and associate individual answer spans with precise, potentially disjoint and hierarchically scoped pixel-level evidence regions instead of coarse bounding boxes?
analyses.methodology: M3Grounder combines a vision-language answer generator with a promptable segmentation module. The language model emits special [GROUND] tokens after answer spans, and each corresponding hidden state is projected through separate phrase-, line-, and block-level heads to prompt segmentation masks for that span. Training combines language-modeling loss, Dice/BCE segmentation supervision, a bleed-suppression objective that penalizes masks extending into irrelevant background, and a hierarchy loss enforcing phrase-within-line-within-block containment. The accompanying GroundingDocQA resource is described as containing 200K documents and 2M QA pairs, while the human-verified GroundingDocQA-Bench contains 2.5K documents and 5K QA pairs.

key_findings.finding: Interleaving answer spans with [GROUND] tokens creates an explicit one-to-one link from each generated span to its own segmentation evidence region, including answers requiring multiple spatially separated regions.
The method predicts evidence at phrase, line, and block levels and constrains those masks hierarchically rather than exposing only one fixed grounding granularity.

GroundingDocQA is described as providing 200K documents and 2M multi-span, multi-granular QA pairs with pixel-level evidence masks, and GroundingDocQA-Bench as providing 2.5K documents and 5K human-verified QA pairs.
key_findings.section: Abstract and official project dataset description

key_findings.finding: The official benchmark table reports M3Grounder-Q scores of 81.4 F1g on BD-Test, 73.3 F1g on DOGR-Bench, 68.2 IoU on MMDocBench, and 79.0 F1g on GroundingDocQA-Bench, exceeding the compared systems in that table.
For M3Grounder-Q, the official multi-granularity results report 80.1 phrase F1, 84.3 line F1, and 87.5 block F1.
The paper presents segmentation masks as an alternative to rectangular grounding because masks can follow curved or irregular text and avoid including unrelated background inside a box.

limitations: The accessible CVF HTML record exposed the abstract rather than the complete paper, and direct full-PDF retrieval returned HTTP 403, so detailed paper-stated limitations and all ablations could not be independently checked from the full manuscript.

At access time, the official project page still labeled the dataset and models as 'Soon', while its Code link resolved to the project-page repository rather than a training or inference implementation.
The provenance target is a pixel region within a document image; attachment identity, attachment revision history, and cross-version evidence lineage are not modeled.
The evaluation centers on grounded document QA rather than email threads or longitudinal workplace communication in which the same attachment may be revised.
raw_claims: M3Grounder formulates document evidence grounding as pixel-level segmentation rather than bounding-box generation.
Generated answers contain [GROUND] tokens linking individual answer spans to evidence masks.
A single answer can contain multiple independently grounded evidence spans.
The system predicts phrase-, line-, and block-level evidence masks.
A hierarchy objective encourages phrase masks to be enclosed by line masks and line masks by block masks.
A bleed-suppression loss penalizes masks that spill into irrelevant regions.
GroundingDocQA is described as containing 200K documents and 2M grounded QA pairs.
GroundingDocQA-Bench is described as human verified and explicitly evaluates multi-span and multi-granular grounding.
The official results page reports stronger grounding scores for M3Grounder than the compared baselines across the displayed grounding benchmarks.
The current official artifact page does not yet expose the announced dataset and model releases.

analyses.title: Scene-Text Oriented Referring Expression Comprehension
analyses.research_question: Can referring-expression comprehension be improved by explicitly recognizing scene text and aligning the text mentioned in a referring expression with corresponding textual regions in an image?
analyses.methodology: The work defines scene-text oriented referring expression comprehension (ST-REC), in which scene text is treated as a discriminative cue for identifying referred objects. It proposes a Scene Text Awareness Network (STAN) with a correlated text extraction module for identifying semantically relevant scene text and a correlated region activation module for associating that text with relevant image regions while handling missing or ambiguous alignments. The authors also construct the RefText benchmark for quantitative evaluation. The official implementation repository describes RefText as containing about 31K manually generated referring expressions for 11K objects and provides annotations, images, OCR resources, training code, and evaluation code.

key_findings.finding: The paper establishes ST-REC as a task specifically designed to exploit scene text for identifying and disambiguating referred visual objects.
STAN explicitly bridges linguistic references to scene text and the corresponding visual text regions through correlated text extraction and correlated region activation modules.

The accessible abstract reports that STAN effectively handles scene-text-oriented referring expressions and achieves strong experimental performance, although the accessible text does not expose the numerical comparison.
The official repository describes RefText as containing approximately 31K manually generated referring expressions referring to 11K objects from multiple image sources.

limitations: Only an abstract-level version of the paper was accessible, so numerical results, ablations, and the authors' detailed limitations could not be verified from the full text.
The task concerns object localization in natural scenes using scene text rather than document-page structure, tables, email attachments, or workplace-document provenance.
Its grounding target is the referred object or scene-text-related visual region, not a persistent citation such as an attachment version, document page, or table cell identifier.
The supplied 2026 date does not match the accessible bibliographic record, which identifies the article as published online in 2022 and associated with IEEE Transactions on Multimedia volume 25.
raw_claims: Conventional referring-expression comprehension often ignores scene text even though text can identify or disambiguate objects.
The work introduces scene-text oriented referring expression comprehension as a separate task.
STAN is designed to align scene text mentioned in language with scene text visible in the image.
A correlated text extraction module is used to improve semantic understanding of relevant scene text.
A correlated region activation module is used to reduce incorrect or absent alignment between expression text and image regions.
RefText is introduced as a benchmark for quantitative ST-REC evaluation.
The official repository provides an implementation of STAN.
The official repository provides RefText annotations, image resources, and OCR data.
The accessible abstract claims strong experimental performance but does not provide the numerical scores.

analyses.title: RefChartQA: Grounding Visual Answer on Chart Images through Instruction Tuning
analyses.research_question: Can chart question-answering models be instruction-tuned to return both an answer and the precise chart elements supporting that answer, and does this explicit spatial grounding improve answer reliability?
analyses.methodology: RefChartQA extends ChartQA and a subset of TinyChart's ChartQA-PoT data with explicit bounding-box evidence annotations generated through three stages: heuristic single-element matching, Program-of-Thought-based extraction, and GPT-4o-mini-based annotation for harder cases, with answer validation used to reject inconsistent annotations. The resulting benchmark contains 73,702 image-question-grounding pairs split into 55,789 training, 6,223 validation, and 11,690 test examples. Models are instruction-tuned to generate one or more ordered bounding boxes, with coordinates normalized and quantized to the range [0,1000), followed by the textual answer. Evaluation separates answer correctness from grounding quality using relaxed ChartQA accuracy, AP@0.5, and P@FI, the latter requiring all evidence boxes for a sample to be correct.

key_findings.finding: Manual checking of 50 samples from each split by two annotators yielded 93.45% agreement on grounding correctness, while also revealing cases with multiple defensible grounding regions.

Grounding instruction tuning produced large answer-accuracy gains for some models: TinyChart improved by 17.42 points on the human split and 15.36 on the PoT split, while Qwen-VL-Chat improved by 22.94 points on the PoT split.

A universal claim that grounding always improves answer accuracy is contradicted by Table 2: UniChart loses accuracy on all three splits, ChartGemma loses substantially on the human and PoT splits, and Qwen2.5-VL declines on the human and machine-generated splits.

Grounding becomes substantially harder as reasoning complexity increases: reported P@FI is roughly 70-84% on mostly simple machine-generated questions, about 40-70% on PoT questions, and about 22-50% on human-authored questions.
Correct visual localization does not guarantee a correct answer because models sometimes identify the right chart elements but fail at the subsequent mathematical reasoning.
The suggestion that architecture is more important than pretraining corpus for grounding is explicitly tentative; the authors state that controlled experimentation is still required to validate it.

limitations: The authors identify limited data diversity and uncertain generalization to noisier and more varied real-world chart designs.
Grounding labels can be inconsistent because standardized annotation guidelines are lacking and some questions admit multiple valid evidence regions.
The role of architecture in benefiting from visual answer grounding remains underexplored and requires controlled experiments.
Bounding boxes provide region-level provenance inside a chart image but do not identify a stable document page, attachment, or attachment version.
The annotation pipeline can inherit errors from ChartQA and ChartQA-PoT and can introduce additional mistakes during automated grounding annotation.
Complex multi-element numerical reasoning remains considerably more difficult than simple single-element grounding.
raw_claims: RefChartQA augments chart question answering with explicit visual evidence grounding.
Its annotation pipeline combines heuristic matching, program-derived evidence extraction, and LLM-assisted annotation.
Candidate annotations are validated against the expected answer before being retained.
The benchmark contains 73,702 annotated image-question-grounding examples.
Grounding boxes are serialized together with the generated answer so existing autoregressive VLMs can be instruction-tuned without a separate detection head.
P@FI treats a sample as correct only when all required evidence regions are correctly grounded.
Some models gain more than fifteen accuracy points after grounding training.
Other evaluated models lose answer accuracy after grounding training, so the benefit is not universal.
Human-authored and multi-element reasoning questions are much harder to ground than simple machine-generated questions.
A model can localize the correct evidence but still calculate the wrong answer.
Some questions permit several reasonable grounding regions even though the benchmark annotation selects a particular reference.
The authors regard architectural explanations for grounding performance as a hypothesis needing further controlled study.

analyses.title: Hierarchical multimodal transformers for Multi-Page DocVQA
analyses.research_question: Can a hierarchical multimodal transformer answer questions over entire multi-page documents while preserving enough page structure to identify the page containing the supporting evidence?
analyses.methodology: The authors create MP-DocVQA, containing 46,176 questions over 5,928 documents and 47,952 page images, with documents represented using OCR text, two-dimensional layout information, and visual features. Hi-VT5 processes every page separately with a T5-based encoder and compresses question-conditioned page information into learnable [PAGE] tokens; summaries from all pages are concatenated for answer generation and for an auxiliary answer-page classifier. A hierarchical layout-aware denoising objective pretrains the [PAGE] representations, followed by MP-DocVQA training on shortened two-page documents and a final full-document fine-tuning phase. Evaluation reports answer accuracy, ANLS, and answer-page identification accuracy.

key_findings.finding: MP-DocVQA contains 46,176 questions over 5,928 documents and 47,952 page images, creating a substantially longer-input document-QA setting than single-page DocVQA.
In the realistic multi-page setting, Hi-VT5 achieved 48.28 answer accuracy, 0.6201 ANLS, and 79.23% answer-page accuracy, outperforming the evaluated multi-page baseline configurations.
Conventional concatenation baselines suffer increasingly when the answer occurs late in a document, whereas the performance gap in favor of Hi-VT5 becomes larger for later answer-page positions.
Hierarchical denoising pretraining provides the largest answering boost in the ablation study: removing it drops accuracy from 48.28 to 42.10 and ANLS from 0.6201 to 0.5864.

Joint page identification provides provenance useful for diagnosing unsupported answers: the authors observe cases where an answer is correct but the predicted evidence page is wrong, indicating reliance on learned prior bias rather than the actual source page.

Compression into [PAGE] summaries loses some information: in the oracle single-answer-page setting Hi-VT5 scores 50.01 accuracy and 0.6572 ANLS versus 59.00 and 0.6814 for T5 with access to the full page representation.

limitations: Evidence provenance is only page-level; the system does not identify the precise supporting cell, text span, bounding box, or image region inside the predicted page.
The benchmark and final classifier are designed for documents of up to 20 pages, so behavior on substantially longer documents is not established.
Although inference can accept long inputs, training memory grows with the number of pages because each page is encoded separately, motivating two-page training followed by full-length fine-tuning.
Compressing a page into a small set of [PAGE] tokens discards information, as shown by the lower oracle performance relative to T5 using the full answer page.
The approach depends on OCR-derived textual and layout features in addition to document-image features.
Page identification does not represent attachment identity or attachment-version lineage, so it cannot by itself distinguish evidence from successive revisions of the same workplace document.
raw_claims: MP-DocVQA extends document visual question answering from isolated pages to complete multi-page documents.
The dataset contains 46,176 questions associated with 5,928 documents and 47,952 page images.
Hi-VT5 independently encodes each page and summarizes question-relevant information into learned [PAGE] tokens.
The decoder generates an answer from the concatenated page summaries.
A separate prediction head identifies the page expected to contain the answer evidence.
The architecture can accept up to 20,480 input tokens without increasing its parameter count with document length.
Hierarchical layout-aware denoising pretraining substantially improves answer performance.
Long-sequence baselines remain vulnerable when the relevant answer appears near the end of the document.
The compact page representation performs worse than full-page T5 when an oracle supplies the correct page.
Correct answers paired with incorrect page predictions expose cases that may derive from learned priors rather than grounded document evidence.
The authors publicly released the dataset, baselines, model code, and weights.
